implementation_notes: Foundation gives every thread a dictionary: Thread.current.threadDictionary is an NSMutableDictionary owned by the thread, documented in Apple's threading guide as the place to keep state that must persist throughout the thread's execution (Cocoa and POSIX maintain separate stores, so the two must not be mixed). The classic key/collection/proxy structure is replaced by that dictionary plus a typed accessor; values are stored as Any and nothing is cleaned up when the work item ends. Under Swift concurrency this is the wrong storage - tasks are not bound to threads - which is why @TaskLocal is the modern realization; the dictionary remains the tool for classic thread-per-request code and for libraries that predate Swift concurrency.
pitfalls: The dictionary is untyped (Any) and never cleaned up: a value set on a pooled thread stays alive and visible to whatever runs on that thread next, so remove it explicitly at the end of the unit of work.

Under Swift 6 strict concurrency, accessing Thread.threadDictionary from different isolation domains is a data race: threads are not the unit Swift concurrency schedules, so this storage cannot cross an await.
Cocoa's thread dictionary and POSIX pthread_setspecific storage are independent stores; mixing them in one thread silently loses values.

variants.name: @TaskLocal (task-scoped ambient value)
variants.implementation_notes: A @TaskLocal property is declared once (static, and global since Swift 6), read as an ordinary property, and bound only through the scoped $property.withValue(_:) call: the value is visible for the dynamic extent of that scope and to child tasks created inside it (TaskGroup, async let, unstructured Task), is not inherited by detached tasks, and cannot be set directly. The runtime carries the binding with the task instead of the thread and falls back to thread-local storage when a value is bound outside any task, so it replaces Thread.threadDictionary for every async path while remaining usable from synchronous code.
pitfalls: Detached tasks do not inherit task-local values, and unstructured Task {} copies them at creation time only - values bound afterwards are not seen.
The property must be static (or global); declaring it as an instance property is a compile-time error because the key is the property wrapper's identity.
Values are readable only inside withValue and default to the declared default elsewhere, so work that outlives the scope silently reads the default instead of the bound value.
Stored values must be Sendable: holding a mutable reference object defeats the isolation and trips strict-concurrency checking.
